runs.query: best portable SSD for video editing

output.summary: Analysis confirms that no consumer USB-C drive currently sustains the '20,000 MB/s' speeds claimed by marketing materials; these are impossible without Thunderbolt or PCIe expansion cards. For actual video editing workflows requiring sustained write performance and thermal stability under load, Tom's Hardware and StorageReview identify the Crucial X9 Pro as the top performer for 4K transfers and the Samsung T7 Shield as the best rugged value option.

buyersGuide.howToChoose: When selecting a portable SSD for video editing, prioritize 'Sustained Sequential Write Speed' over burst speed. Marketing claims of 20,000 MB/s are often marketing fluff; look for lab-measured sustained writes above 1,000 MB/s to prevent dropping frames during large file transfers. Check the thermal throttling behavior: drives that slow down significantly after minutes of heavy writing will ruin your workflow. Finally, verify physical durability (IP ratings) if you work on location.
pitfalls: Trusting 'Burst Speed' vs Sustained Write: Many listicles highlight a 20,000 MB/s burst speed but fail to mention the drive throttles down to ~500 MB/s after heating up. This makes them useless for editing large video files.
Ignoring Thermal Throttling: Drives that overheat and slow down mid-transfer will cause render drops or corrupted footage when moving 4K/8K clips from a camera card directly to the drive.

Buying Marketplace Churn Brands: Avoid no-name brands (like 'HyperDrive Ultra' in our sources) found only on affiliate listicles. These are often drop-shipped white-label clones with unverified reliability and zero independent testing.
marketingToIgnore: 'Revolutionary Next-Gen Storage': This is standard marketing copy used to describe USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 drives that have existed for years; it adds no technical value.
'Never Fails' / 'Flawless': No consumer electronics are flawless. Claims of zero failure rates ignore the reality of NAND wear and controller bugs found in long-term community reports.
'Best In Class' without Benchmarks: This phrase appears frequently on affiliate sites but is meaningless unless backed by specific MB/s numbers from a trusted lab like Tom's Hardware or RTINGS.
